items.description: The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) uses a science-based, adaptive framework for setting and achieving broad-scale conservation objectives that strategically address the problems fish and wildlife will face in the future. This framework, called Strategic Habitat Conservation, is based on the principles of adaptive management and uses population and habitat data, ecological models, and focused monitoring and assessment efforts to develop and implement strategies that result in measurable fish and wildlife population outcomes. This process uses the best available scientific information to predict how fish and wildlife populations will respond to changes in the environment, thus enabling the USFWS to focus habitat conservation and other management activities where they will be most effective. In addition, the USFWS needs focused, applied science directed at high impact questions surrounding threats to fish and wildlife resources for which management and/or mitigation is required to maintain species at healthy, sustainable, desired levels. USFWS must base its decisions on the best science available, in order to defend its regulatory decisions, biological opinions and species…

items.uses: Support will be provided for science projects: to include species risk and vulnerability assessments, inventory and monitoring, population and habitat assessments, biological planning and conservation design, ecosystem services, indigenous knowledge management evaluation and research, decision support, data management, and conservation genetics; to identify and implement landscape-scale conservation solutions to such issues as adaptation, land use change, invasive species spread, and fire frequency changes; and to address high impact questions surrounding threats to fish wildlife, and plants, providing answers needed to manage species to healthy, sustainable, desired levels. These are discretionary funds that are used for project purposes to help ensure the use of the best available scientific information in making management decisions. Funding can be used for construction activities. Funding is not used for real property acquisition under this program.

items.title: Experienced Services
items.summary: Enable the agency to work with select NGOs to fill a wide variety of temporary human resource needs with skilled, experienced workers, aged 55 and older, while also providing opportunities to qualified older Americans to have meaningful work and fair wages.
items.description: The Experienced Services Program offers a flexible option for the US Fish and Wildlife Service to complete targeted priority projects and fill in administrative or program needs by using the services of experienced workers across all sectors of business. This program awards cooperative agreements to two nonprofit partner organizations who provide recruitment and staffing services as requested by the Service. Each agreement funds the work of one or more enrollees, aged 55+, who are selected for their experience, knowledge, and skills to complete tasks and projects which the Service would otherwise be unable to complete. These enrollees are able to fill critical gaps in staffing, and allow the Service to carry out its mission.
items.who: Applicants must be nonprofits and eligible to receive funds from the Department of Labor under Title V of the Older Americans Act (Senior Community Service Employment Program).
items.uses: Recipients will use funding to cover overhead or administrative costs to fulfill its obligations under the cooperative agreement, as well as salary and benefits for enrollees. Overhead or administrative costs may include payroll and benefits management, required reporting, and providing interactive portal for enrollee supervisors, among others.

items.title: Prescott Marine Mammal Rescue Assistance
items.summary: To provide financial assistance to eligible entities for: response, recovery, rescue, treatment, and, as appropriate, release of West Indian manatees, sea otters, Pacific walruses, and polar bears; the collection of data for scientific research associated with the health of these species; and facility operation costs for these species, as appropriate.
items.description: The Marine Mammal Protection Act authorizes the Secretary of the Interior to carry out a grant program to provide financial assistance to rescue and respond to stranded marine mammals. Specifically, this program provides critical funding to entities that recover, care, and treat sick, injured, or entangled marine mammals; respond to marine mammal stranding events that require emergency assistance; and collect data and samples from living or dead stranded marine mammals for scientific research or assessments regarding marine mammal health. The grant program also supports facility operating costs and the development of stranding network capacity, including training for emergency response, where facilities do not exist or are sparse. The Prescott Grant Program has been very successful in providing vital funding to support polar bear, sea otter, walrus, and manatee rescue and rehabilitation efforts across the country.
items.who: Applicants must be a U.S. eligible marine mammal stranding participant or stranding network collaborator that is not an employee of the Department of the Interior or Department of Commerce. The term “eligible marine mammal stranding participant” means a person who is authorized by the FWS under MMPA section 104(c) for response to injured or distressed marine mammals or for scientific research regarding marine mammal health, or under MMPA section 112(c) to take marine mammals as described in MMPA section 109(h) in response to a stranding. Eligible entities also include Federal, state, or local government employees operating in the course of their official duties as indicated under MMPA…
items.uses: Funds will be awarded to and must be used by recipients for: response, recovery, rescue, treatment, and, as appropriate, release of marine mammals under the management jurisdiction of the Service (i.e., West Indian manatees, sea otters, Pacific walruses, and polar bears); the collection of data for scientific research associated with the health of these marine mammal species; and facility operation costs, as appropriate.

items.title: White-nose Syndrome National Response Implementation
items.summary: The goal of White-nose Syndrome National Response Implementation is to conserve and recover bat species affected by the fungal disease white-nose syndrome (WNS) through partnership driven management, research and communication. WNS Grants to States and Tribes support agencies and organizations for management planning and actions, coordination of research activities, and collaboration with partners around…
items.description: The White-nose Syndrome National Response provides the framework for a broad partnership of government and non-government entities engaged in bat conservation and management. The partnership comprises federal, state, tribal, provincial agencies and non-government organizations and institutions across North America and beyond contributing to cross-border coordination, research, pathogen and disease surveillance, disease management, information sharing, and public engagement. A primary federal role is to provide funding for State wildlife management agencies to address bat conservation and WNS-related needs. WNS Grants to States and Tribes provide funding to wildlife agencies and departments conducting research and management of hibernating bat species. Funding through this opportunity supports local management of bats with cross-jurisdiction coordination to leverage efforts among partners. This grant program helps partners maintain staff dedicated to management of bats and supports their completion of projects that have lasting benefits to bat species and reduce the potential for federal regulatory action in the future. Cooperative agreements and WNS Research for Conservation…
items.who: Eligibility varies by funding opportunity.
items.uses: Funds must be used for projects that align with and support the WNS National Response Plan, including the priorities and efforts identified within that context. Such actions include management activities of state and tribal wildlife and natural resource agencies and departments working to combat the disease and conserve species affected by it. Congress appropriated these funds to the Service for the purpose of implementing the National Response to White-nose Syndrome, through which the North American Bat Monitoring Program was formed. The Service will identify any restrictions on use of the assistance under this program in the Funding Opportunity Announcements posted in GrantSolutions and Grants.gov, as applicable. 100% of program funds are discretionary.
contacts: Jeremy Coleman, National Coordinator for White-Nose Syndrome · 413-253-8223 · Jeremy_Coleman@fws.gov

items.title: National Fish Passage
items.summary: To restore native fish and other aquatic species to self-sustaining levels by reconnecting habitat that barriers have fragmented, where such reconnection would not result in a net negative ecological effect such as providing increased habitat to aquatic nuisance species. Fish passage projects restore unimpeded flows and fish movement by removing barriers or providing ways for aquatic species to bypass them; such…
items.description: The National Fish Passage Program (NFPP) is a voluntary cooperative conservation program administered by the U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service (USFWS) that provides financial and technical assistance to reconnect aquatic habitats fragmented by barriers such as culverts and outdated infrastructure. Millions of aging barriers across the country fragment rivers, block fish migration, and increase flood risk to farms and communities. Removing them upgrades failing infrastructure, restores productive fishing waters, and expands public access for recreation, hunting, and fishing; all while benefiting farmers, rural communities, and local economies. What sets the NFPP apart is its cooperative, partnership-driven model. Rather than functioning as a traditional grant program, the USFWS works directly with partners to identify and fund the highest-priority projects, relying on a nationwide network of biologists and engineers at Fish and Wildlife Conservation Offices. Funding is open to federal and state agencies, Tribes, non-governmental organizations, ranchers, and private landowners for project types including culvert replacements, floodplain restoration, fishway installation, low-water…
items.who: Entities must be willing and able to implement program projects collaboratively with the Service.
items.uses: Assistance may be used for approved projects restoring or preserving fish passage and aquatic habitat connectivity including construction, design/engineering, and support of fish passage projects.

items.title: National Fish Habitat Partnership
items.summary: To comprehensively address the causes of fish habitat decline by working together with partners to maximize the impact of limited funding for fish habitat conservation. Under NFHP, Federal, State, Tribal, and privately-raised funds are leveraged through 20 Fish Habitat Partnerships to address the fish habitat challenges. More information about the Fish Habitat Partnerships and their partners can be found online at…
items.description: This Assistance Listing for the National Fish Habitat Partnership Program was established in FY24. Awards made prior to FY23 were reported under Assistance Listing 15.608. This Assistance Listing for the National Fish Habitat Partnership provides funding for the coordination of fish habitat conservation work conducted by state, federal, tribal, non-profit, and private entities to increase efficiency and improve outcomes by leveraging resources among partners working through 20 Congressionally-designated Fish Habitat Partnerships.
items.who: Limited to entities associated with a Fish Habitat Partnership recognized by the National Fish Habitat Partnership Board.
items.uses: Assistance may be used only for aquatic habitat conservation projects recommended by a recognized Fish Habitat Partnership, the National Fish Habitat Partnership Board and selected by the Secretary of the Interior. Assistance may be used for construction as described in a project proposal selected by the National Fish Habitat Partnership Board. Assistance may be used for real property acquisition provided the acquisition has been approved by the State agency in the State in which the project is occurring.

items.title: Great Lakes Sea Lamprey Control
items.summary: To work with partners to assess sea lamprey abundance in the Great Lakes by monitoring the spring spawning migration in tributaries. Population assessments allow the Service to estimate the index of adult sea lampreys and evaluate the success of the Sea Lamprey Control Program. To work with partners to access reservation lands and complete sea lamprey larval assessment and lampricide treatment activities.
items.description: This Assistance Listing for the Great Lakes Sea Lamprey Control program was established in FY24.
items.who: Directed Announcements focused on specific recipients with authority and expertise in Great Lakes Sea Lamprey Control.
items.uses: Funds may be used to assess sea lamprey abundance in the Great Lakes by monitoring the spring spawning migration in specific tributaries, assess sea lamprey larval abundance, and deliver lampricide treatment activities in Great Lakes tributaries.

items.summary: To provide assistance to States, Indian Tribes, and other interested entities to encourage cooperative conservation, restoration, research, and management of the fish and wildlife resources and their habitats in the Great Lakes Basin.
items.description: This Assistance Listing for the Great Lakes Fish and Wildlife Restoration Act was established in FY24. Awards made prior to FY24 were reported under Assistance Listing 15.608. GLWRA provides assistance to States, Indian Tribes, and other interested entities to encourage cooperative conservation, restoration, research, and management of the fish and wildlife resources and their habitats in the Great Lakes Basin.
items.who: Anyone/general public with eligible research, restoration, and Regional Project proposals for the restoration of the Great Lakes Basin fish and wildlife resources, as described in the program’s Notices of Funding Opportunity on Grants.gov.
items.uses: Funds may be used to conduct fish and wildlife management and research activities that align with the conservation, restoration, and management goals noted in 16 U.S.C. §941 et seq.

items.title: Orangutan and Gibbon Conservation Fund
items.summary: The objectives of this fund are to sustain viable populations of great apes in the wild; and to assist in the conservation and protection of great apes by supporting conservation programs of countries in which populations of great apes are located and by supporting the CITES Secretariat.
items.description: This Assistance Listing was created in FY25. Awards made prior to FY25 were reported under Assistance Listing 15.629. The purpose of this fund is to sustain viable populations of great apes in the wild and to assist in the conservation and protection of great apes by supporting conservation programs of countries in which populations of great apes are located and by supporting the CITES Secretariat.
items.who: Applications may be submitted by any entity responsible for conservation and protection of orangutans and gibbons and any other organization or individual with demonstrated experience in orangutan and gibbon conservation.
items.uses: Funds provided under this program support projects that will enhance programs for conservation of great apes by assisting efforts to: (1) implement conservation programs; (2) address the conflicts between humans and great apes that arise from competition for the same habitat; (3) enhance compliance with CITES and other applicable laws that prohibit or regulate the taking or trade of great apes or regulate the use and management of great ape habitat; (4) develop sound scientific information on, or methods for monitoring—(A) the condition and health of great ape habitat; (B) great ape population numbers and trends; or (C) the current and projected threats to the habitat, current and projected numbers, or current and projected trends; or (5) promote cooperative projects on the issues among government entities, affected local communities, nongovernmental organizations, or other persons in…

items.title: Rhinoceros Conservation Fund
items.summary: Provide financial assistance for projects for the effective, long-term conservation of African rhino populations and their habitats. The objectives are to increase population growth, management and governance improvements at key rhino sites, and to develop greater national leadership and capacity, stakeholder collaboration, and effective CITES implementation in key rhino range states. This program supports projects…

The objective of the fund is to assist in the conservation of rhinoceros by supporting the conservation programs of nations whose activities directly or indirectly affect rhinoceros populations, and the CITES Secretariat, to provide financial resources for those programs, and to prohibit the sale, importation, and exportation of products intended for human consumption or application containing, or labeled or advertised as containing, any substance derived from any species of rhinoceros.
items.who: Funds provided under this program support projects that will enhance programs for conservation of rhinoceros or tigers by assisting efforts to— (1) implement conservation programs; (2) enhance compliance with provisions of CITES and laws of the United States or a foreign country that prohibit or regulate the taking or trade of rhinoceros or the use of rhinoceros habitat; or (3) develop sound scientific information on that species' habitat condition and carrying capacity, total numbers and population trends, or annual reproduction and mortality.

items.title: Nicodemus National Historic Site
items.summary: The town of Nicodemus, in Kansas, has national significance as the only remaining western town established by African-Americans during the Reconstruction period following the Civil War. The town of Nicodemus is symbolic of the pioneer spirit of African-Americans who dared to leave the only region they had been familiar with to seek personal freedom and the opportunity to develop their talents and capabilities. The…
items.description: This program provides funding to preserve, protect, and interpret the historic structures and sites in Nicodemus, Kansas—the only remaining western town established by African Americans during Reconstruction. items.uses: To further the preservation, protection, and interpretation of the history and town of Nicodemus, KS.

items.summary: To provide financial support to Water Resources Research Institutes located at designated State universities in each of the 50 States, Puerto Rico, the District of Columbia, Guam, the Virgin Islands, American Samoa, the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, and the Federated States of Micronesia for research, information transfer and student training on one or more aspects of priority water problems.
items.description: The Water Resources Research Act established a federal-state partnership to support water research, technology transfer and training through each state- or territory-based research institutes. The USGS Water Resources Research Act program works directly with each designated Water Resource Research Institute in each U.S. State and Territory.
items.who: One University Water Research Institute is authorized in each State and other jurisdictions specified in Section 104. Other colleges and universities within a State are encouraged to participate in the program in cooperation with the designated Institute.
items.uses: This program has two parts: a mandatory formula grant program and a competitive project grant program. The mandatory grant program provides the State Institutes with funds to support a State and regional program of water resources research and information transfer. This may include basic or applied research, setting up conferences to discuss research needs or results, conduct of research, information dissemination, and training of students as a byproduct of research. In general the funds are used to study regional, State, or local water problems, but the results may often have national significance. The competitive project grant program supports research focused on water problems of a regional or interstate nature and which relate to program priorities identified jointly by the State Institutes and the Geological Survey. items.title: National Cooperative Geologic Mapping
items.summary: To produce geologic maps of areas in which knowledge of geology is important to the economic, social, or scientific welfare of individual States. StateMap supports: (1) projects which produce new geologic maps with attendant explanatory information including correlation of map units, description of map units and symbols, stratigraphic columns, geologic sections, and other pertinent information; and (2) projects…
items.description: The National Cooperative Geologic Mapping Program (NCGMP) is the primary source of funding for geologic map production in the United States. The NCGMP funds geologic mapping activities through its FEDMAP, STATEMAP, and EDMAP components. This Assistance Listing facilitates cooperative agreements for both STATEMAP and EDMAP. Through STATEMAP, state partners produce geologic data to contribute to a national geologic framework driven by areas of economic, social, or scientific interest. STATEMAP mapping priorities are established by State Geological Surveys in consultation with a multi-representational State Mapping Advisory Committee. These priorities are based on multiple factors including a) state requirements for geologic-map information in areas of multiple-issue need or areas of compelling single-issue need, and b) state requirements for geologic-map information in areas where mapping is required to solve critical earth-science problems. STATEMAP-funded activities focus primarily on geologic maps to address land-use, water resources, aggregate and mineral resources, oil and gas, and natural hazards issues. As the educational component of the National Cooperative Geologic Mapping…
items.who: StateMap program is restricted by statue to State geological surveys. Where State surveys are organized under a State university system, an application may be submitted by a State college or university on behalf of the State geological survey. EdMap program is restricted to universities with geoscience or related departments or programs.
items.uses: STATEMAP: Only one application will be accepted from each State geological survey. State proposals cannot include in-kind services by the U.S. Geological Survey. Travel to meetings of professional societies is not an acceptable expense for the program, nor are funds intended for the purchase of computer hardware, software, or other nonexpendable property. Student tuition or reimbursement is not an allowable expense. EdMap: Proposals cannot include a request for in-kind services by the U.S. Geological Survey. Funds are not intended for the purchase of capital equipment. Student tuition or reimbursement is not an allowable expense. For further information, please contact the National Cooperative Geologic Mapping Program office.

items.title: Cooperative Research Units
items.summary: To work in partnership with States and universities to address the information needs of local, State, and Federal fish, wildlife, and natural resource agencies through research, technical assistance, and education.
items.description: This listing supports research efforts conducted through the U.S. Geological Survey’s Cooperative Research Units Program to inform management and stewardship of fish and wildlife resources for the benefit and enjoyment of all U.S. citizens. The Cooperative Research Units were established with a trifold mission that is codified in the program's authorizing legislation: • Graduate Education - Provide advance training in fish, wildlife, and natural resource sciences, assuring a continuing supply of quality natural resource professionals for state and federal agencies. • Applied Research – Provide federal and state agencies access to the expertise, and facilities at leading universities around the country, to address the natural resource information needs expressed by Unit cooperators and partners. • Technical Assistance - Provide technical assistance in the understanding and use of science and research findings to State and Federal personnel and other natural resource managers.
items.who: Universities hosting Cooperative Fish and Wildlife Research Units established under authority of the Cooperative Research Units Act of 1960.
items.uses: Authority is limited to research with an educational component conducted through one of 40 Cooperative Fish and Wildlife Research Units and their host universities. Awards are limited to information needs related to fish, wildlife, ecology, and natural resources of interest to program cooperators and partners.

items.title: National Geological and Geophysical Data Preservation
items.summary: To preserve and provide access to geological, geophysical, and engineering samples (and any related data) extracted from the Earth to improve the breadth of information available and to inform science and decision making now and in the future.
items.description: The National Geological and Geophysical Data Preservation Program (NGGDPP) was established in 2005 in the Energy Policy Act. The goal of the NGGDPP is to preserve the Nation’s geoscience collections (samples, logs, maps, data) to promote their discovery, use and reuse into the future. The mission of the NGGDPP is to provide access to samples and data to improve the breadth of information that can be used to inform decision making for the nation. The target audience for financial assistance through the NGGDPP is the State Geological Surveys. Their participation is essential to advancing the NGGDPP mission by preserving critical data and ensuring geological resources are accessible to the public through the national catalog called the Registry of Scientific Collections (ReSciColl)
items.who: State geological surveys are eligible to apply. For State geological surveys organized under a State university system, such universities may submit a proposal on behalf of or through the State geological survey.
items.uses: Sample and Data Preservation. Specific objectives are identified in the annual program announcement. items.summary: To promote the uses of space-based land remote sensing data and technologies through education and outreach at the State and local level and through university based and collaborative research projects. Technologies of interest include multispectral and hyper-spectral electro-optical, thermal, and radar.
items.description: This listing conducts nationwide remote sensing, Earth observation, and Geospatial (RS/EO/GS) information gathering activities. Information gathering activities occur at all levels (local, regional, and national), in all relevant industry and commercial areas, and within the academic and research spaces. These activities provide user stories about specific RS/EO/GS use cases, novel applications and approaches, educational needs, and a continuing assessment of how value-added products and applications are supporting a wide variety of user communities.

items.title: National Geospatial Program: Building The National Map
items.summary: The National Map is a collaborative effort among the USGS and other Federal, State, Universities, and local partners to improve and deliver topographic information for the Nation. The 3D National Topography Model, including the 3D Elevation Program (3DEP) and the 3D Hydrography Program (3DHP), is an initiative that updates, improves, and integrates USGS elevation and hydrography data to support the most demanding…
items.description: The U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) National Geospatial Program provides opportunities for partnering with the USGS and other Federal agencies to acquire high-resolution 3D elevation and 3D hydrography data to support the 3D National Topography Model (3DNTM). The collaboration across the Nation responds to a growing need for high-quality elevation and hydrography data which benefit society in array of critically significant applications such as flood-risk management, natural-hazard evaluation and mitigation, and agriculture. The USGS collaborates with State, Tribal, local, academic, and private sector partners to acquire data which are made publicly available and form the base of the elevation and hydrography components of The National Map.
items.who: Proposals from State, Local, Interstate, Federally or State recognized Indian Tribal Governments, US Territories and Possessions, Institutions of Higher Education, Private Foundations, and Nonprofit Organizations are invited. Due to limited availability of funding to support new external projects, consultation with the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) is strongly recommended prior to submission of applications.
items.uses: Applications must be for data collection and research projects which are consistent with the objectives of the National Geospatial Program. The majority of funds are used to support new data collections that will enhance The National Map and to research new methods to use those data. For further information, please contact the headquarters office. For further information, please contact the regional office.

items.title: Volcano Hazards Program Research and Monitoring
items.summary: To advance the scientific understanding of volcanic processes and to lessen the harmful impacts of volcanic activity. The Volcano Hazards Program (VHP) monitors active and potentially active volcanoes, assesses their hazards, responds to volcanic crises, and conducts research on how volcanoes work to fulfill a Congressional mandate (Public Law 93-288) that the USGS issue "timely warnings" of potential volcanic…
items.description: The Volcano Hazards Research and Monitoring Program supports long standing partnerships with state geological surveys and university collaborators that work with the five U.S. volcano observatories. These partners provide specialized scientific expertise and on the ground capabilities essential for monitoring and studying volcanic activity in Alaska, Hawaii, Oregon, Washington, and Wyoming (Yellowstone). Their work generates critical data used by the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) to meet its Congressional mandate to deliver timely and reliable warnings of potential volcanic hazards that threaten public safety. This assistance strengthens the nation’s ability to understand, detect, and respond to volcanic unrest by ensuring that research, monitoring, and hazard assessments are informed by the best available science. It uniquely supports cooperative agreements with established regional experts whose long term knowledge of local volcanic systems contributes directly to national risk reduction efforts. The program also advances the goals of the National Volcano Early Warning and Monitoring System (Public Law 116 9) by prioritizing high threat volcanoes and sustaining the scientific…

items.title: National and Regional Climate Adaptation Science Centers
items.summary: To enable the National and Regional Climate Adaptation Science Centers (NRCASC) to be responsive to the research and management needs of Federal and State agencies.
items.description: The USGS Climate Adaptation Science Centers (CASCs) provide data and information to support cost-effective resource management, hazard risk mitigation, and community resilience across the United States, U.S.-Affiliated Pacific Islands, and U.S. Caribbean. The CASCs work directly with federal, state, tribal, and private sector partners to identify science needs and deliver science products that support strategic resource management decisions that strengthen the nation’s public lands and waters, infrastructure, and economy. The CASCs help resource managers anticipate how future conditions could impact the resources they manage and evaluate the effectiveness of potential management actions, enabling them to make informed, cost-effective decisions.
items.who: There are eight (8) DOI Regional Climate Adaptation Science Centers (RCASC); each CASC has a single "Host Institution" that is eligible to apply on behalf of themselves and members of the CASC university consortium: Alaska CASC: University of Alaska, Fairbanks; Southeast CASC: North Carolina State University, Raleigh; Northwest CASC: University of Washington, Seattle; Southwest CASC: University of Arizona, Tucson; North Central CASC: University of Colorado, Boulder; South Central CASC: Oklahoma University, Norman; Northeast CASC: University of Massachusetts, Amherst; Pacific Islands CASC: University of Hawaii, Manoa.
items.uses: The Department of the Interior (DOI) Regional Climate Adaptation Science Centers were developed according to a consistent national strategy and are managed at the national level by the National Climate Adaptation Science Center (NCASC). NCASC will develop cooperative agreements and/or grants with the DOI CSCs at the primary hosting Universities to conduct specific research, data gathering, data management and similar scientific activities. For further information, please contact the NCASC or Regional DOI CASC office.

Specific objectives and research tasks identified as measures of progress towards the goals of these program elements are described in greater detail in…
items.description: This grant opportunity supports communities that face the risk of landslides by helping them better understand, plan for, and reduce these hazards. It offers funding to state, Tribal, territorial, and local governments so they can strengthen public safety, protect lives and property, and build long‑term resilience. The program focuses on activities that help communities identify where landslides may occur, understand what triggers them, and learn how these events could affect people, infrastructure, and natural resources. It supports efforts such as hazard mapping, data collection, planning, coordination, education, and community outreach, all essential pieces of reducing landslide losses and improving preparedness. What makes this opportunity unique is its emphasis on helping governments use the best available science to guide decisions that keep communities safe. Applicants can pursue projects that improve hazard maps, develop emergency response procedures, train local officials, or engage the public through clear communication and educational materials. These efforts are designed to ensure that the right information reaches the right people at the right time. The program also…

items.title: Economic, Social, and Political Development of the Territories
items.summary: The Office of Insular Affairs carries out the Secretary of the Interior's responsibilities for U.S.-affiliated insular areas. These include the territories of American Samoa, the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands (CNMI), Guam, and the U.S. Virgin Islands (USVI). Additionally, OIA administers and oversees Federal assistance to three freely associated states (FAS): the Federated States of Micronesia (FSM),…
items.description: The Office of Insular Affairs (OIA) carries out the Secretary’s responsibilities for U.S.-affiliated insular areas. These include the territories of American Samoa, the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands (CNMI), Guam, and the U.S. Virgin Islands (USVI). Residents of these U.S. territories are U.S. citizens or U.S. nationals. Additionally, OIA administers and oversees Federal assistance to three freely associated states (FAS): the Federated States of Micronesia (FSM), the Republic of the Marshall Islands (RMI), and the Republic of Palau (Palau). The territories are an integral part of the fabric of America, and the freely associated states, while independent countries, are uniquely interwoven with the United States in terms of a shared history, ongoing partnership, and a shared vision for a free and open Indo-Pacific. Each of the territories and freely associated states are unique, yet their economies are all small, isolated, and dependent on one or two main sources of income. The Office of Insular Affairs has an important role to play in understanding the nuances of the Federal government’s interrelationship with each of the insular areas. OIA facilitates coordination of…

items.summary: To provide grants to museums to assist in the consultation on and documentation of Native American human remains and cultural items; to provide grants to Indian tribes and Native Hawaiian organizations, as defined in the Act, to assist in identifying human remains and cultural items; and to provide grants to museums, Indian tribes and Native Hawaiian organizations to assist in the repatriation of human remains and…
items.description: The Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (NAGPRA) Grants provides funding to help museums, federally recognized Tribes, and Native Hawaiian organizations consult on, document, and return Native American human remains and cultural items with cultural significance. This program supports the repatriation process, covering activities like consultation, travel, transportation, contamination removal, reburial, storage, and related staff time.

[25 USC 3001 (7)]. The…

items.title: National Center for Preservation Technology and Training
items.summary: The purposes of the National Center for Preservation Technology and Training are to— (1) develop and distribute preservation and conservation skills and technologies for the identification, evaluation, conservation, and interpretation of historic property; (2) develop and facilitate training for Federal, State, and local resource preservation professionals, cultural resource managers, maintenance personnel, and…
items.description: This program supports projects that develop innovative tools, materials, and methods for preserving historic buildings, landscapes, and cultural resources across the United States. The National Park Service’s National Center for Preservation Technology and Training (NCPTT) partners with public institutions, governments, and educational organizations to advance the field of preservation and make new technologies more accessible to practitioners and the public. What makes this program unique is its focus on innovation. Funded projects are expected to push the preservation field forward—developing new methods, adapting emerging technologies, or finding creative ways to share preservation knowledge widely.
items.uses: The NCPTT supports preservation research, technology, and training in archeology, historic architecture, historic landscapes, objects preservation and materials conservation through cooperative agreements and grants. Projects that develop new technologies or adapt existing technologies to preserve cultural resources are considered for funding. Projects may include, but are not limited to: laboratory or field research that explores or assesses novel or adaptive methods; training activities, including workshops, webinars, instructional videos, and course or curriculum development that promote the use of new technology in preservation; documentation using new methods; manuscript, website or social media development that disseminates innovative preservation technologies; and meetings that convene experts to discuss the use of technologies to address preservation problems.
contacts: National Center for Preservation Training and Technology · (318) 356-7444 · NCPTT@nps.gov

items.title: National Maritime Heritage Grants
items.summary: The National Maritime Heritage Grants Program provides matching grants for education and preservation projects designed to preserve historic maritime resources and to increase public awareness and appreciation for the maritime heritage of the United States. The grants will help State, Tribal, and local governments and private nonprofit organizations preserve and interpret their maritime heritage.
items.description: The National Maritime Heritage Grants provide 1-to-1 matching funds for a wide range of preservation and education projects in three broad categories: Historic Maritime Properties, Maritime Heritage Collections, and Traditional Maritime Skills. Grant projects are intended to help preserve our historic maritime resources and to promote and educate the public about America's extensive maritime heritage legacy.
items.who: Any State Historic Preservation Office (SHPO) in a state, territory, or freely associated state as well as the National Trust for Historic Preservation can apply for a National Maritime Heritage grant. Once they've received a grant they become known as the prime recipient. The prime recipient is able to use their grants to operate in-house projects and/or run competitive subgrant programs. State, tribal, or local governments or nonprofit organizations can apply for National Maritime Heritage Grant subgrants. Individuals and federal agencies are not eligible to apply for National Maritime Heritage Maritime grants or subgrants.
items.uses: Funds may be used for education or preservation projects that promote the understanding of significant aspect of American maritime heritage. Projects that involve historic resources as defined in the National Historic Preservation Act, as amended, must comply with treatments defined in the "Secretary of the Interior's Standards for the Treatment of Historic Properties" (36 CFR 78), “Standards for Historic Vessel Preservation Projects”, and “Standards for Archeology and Historic Preservation” (48 FR 44716). The Grantee must grant a preservation easement or preservation agreement for each grant-assisted property. In general, the Grants Program does not fund projects which will train the individual maritime heritage professional to do his or her job better or assist in career recognition or promotion. This includes activities such as developing training or continuing education courses for…

These grants serve state, tribal, and local governments, as well as universities and nonprofit organizations, helping them carry out non-land-acquisition projects that make battlefield history accessible and meaningful to the public.

items.title: Battlefield Land Acquisition Grants
items.summary: To assist States and local communities acquire and preserve threatened battlefield land from the Revolutionary War, War of 1812, and Civil War. This grant program enables the permanent protection of historic battlefield lands through fee simple acquisition or through the purchase of an interest in the land through a preservation covenant.
items.description: Battlefield Land Acquisition Grants support efforts to permanently protect historic battlefield lands from the Revolutionary War, War of 1812, and Civil War. This program provides competitive grants to state and local governments—often working with preservation groups—to acquire battlefield land either by purchasing it outright or through conservation easements. All grants require a dollar-for-dollar non-Federal match, ensuring communities invest alongside the federal contribution.
items.who: States, Tribes, and local governments. Nonprofit organizations seeking to acquire battlefield land or easements must apply in partnership with the State or local government agency that has jurisdiction over the proposed parcel. The government agency may then sub-grant the Federal funds to the nonprofit organization.
items.uses: Grants are available for the fee simple acquisition of land, or for the acquisition of permanent, protective interests in land (easements), at Civil War battlefields listed in the Civil War Sites Advisory Commission's (CWSAC) 1993 "Report on the Nation's Civil War Battlefields" and at Revolutionary War and War of 1812 Battlefields listed in the American Battlefield Protection Program (ABPP) 2007 "Report to Congress on the Historic Preservation of Revolutionary War and War of 1812 Sites in the United States." To be eligible for acquisition, the land must be at least 50% within the boundary of a Revolutionary War, War of 1812 or Civil War battlefield identified in the reports above. Funds may not be used to acquire land or interests in land within the legislative boundary of a unit of the National Park System. items.title: Save America's Treasures
items.summary: To provide matching grants for preservation or conservation work on nationally significant intellectual and cultural artifacts and nationally significant historic structures and sites. Intellectual and cultural artifacts include artifacts, collections, documents, sculpture and works of art.
items.description: Save America's Treasures funds competitive grants that help preserve and share nationally significant historic properties and cultural collections. This program supports two types of projects: 1) Preservation Projects that restore and stabilize buildings, sites, and landmarks listed on the National Register of Historic Places or recognized as National Historic Landmarks; and 2) Collections Projects that conserve important artifacts, documents, artworks, and archival materials held in museums, libraries, archives, and other cultural institutions. These grants serve a broad range of public-interest organizations—including state and local governments, nonprofit cultural organizations, college and university museums, federal agencies, and Tribal entities.
items.who: State and Local agencies, Public or Private nonprofit institutions/organizations, State Colleges and Universities, Public and Private Colleges and Universities, Federally Recognized Indian Tribes, and Federal agencies funded by the Department of the Interior and Related Agencies with the exception of the National Park Service. Individuals are not eligible applicants. Properties receiving Save America's Treasures (SAT) grant assistance must be listed in the National Register of Historic Places for National significance
items.uses: Funds may be used for projects resulting in the protection and preservation of nationally significant historic structures and sites, as well as nationally significant collections of cultural artifacts, documents, sculpture and works of art. Projects must comply with the Secretary of the Interior’s Standards and Guidelines for Archeology and Historic Preservation. No funding is given to projects dealing with acquisition or reconstruction of properties or collections, payment of rent on properties or land, fund-raising, or lobbying. Grantee must execute a preservation easement or preservation agreement for each grant-assisted historic site to the State Historic Preservation Officer (SHPO) for at least 50 years from the end date of the grant agreement.

items.title: Youth and Veteran Organizations Conservation Activities
items.summary: This program seeks to utilize qualified non-profit youth and veteran serving organizations to carry out appropriate natural and cultural resource conservation, education, and volunteer service projects on Department of the Interior lands through authorized National Park Service programs.
items.description: The Youth and Veteran Organizations Conservation Activities program helps young adults and veterans gain hands‑on experience protecting and caring for America’s public lands. Through partnerships with nonprofit and community organizations, the program supports projects that strengthen conservation skills, expand volunteerism, and build pathways to careers in natural and cultural resource stewardship. This program serves youth ages 18–30, veterans up to age 35, and the community organizations that work with them.
items.who: Qualified youth or conservation corps - The term “qualified youth or conservation corps” means any program established by a State or local government, by the governing body of any Indian tribe, or by a nonprofit organization that— (A) is capable of offering meaningful, full-time, productive work for individuals between the ages of 16 and 30, inclusive, or veterans age 35 or younger in a natural or cultural resource setting; (B) gives participants a mix of work experience, basic and life skills, education, training, and support services; and (C) provides participants with the opportunity to develop citizenship values and skills through service to their community and the United States.
items.uses: Funding can be used by organizations to support natural and/or cultural resource conservation projects; youth and young adult vocational/career training; natural/cultural resource conservation focused educational programming; natural resources conservation focused recreation activities.

Many HBCU campuses contain nationally significant historic resources that reflect the history of Black education in the United States. The program supports projects that document, stabilize, repair, and rehabilitate these historic places so they can continue to serve their institutions and communities. The program serves accredited HBCUs that own or steward historic properties listed in, or eligible for listing in, the National Register of Historic Places.

items.description: This program supports efforts to preserve and share the history of the mass removal and incarceration of Japanese Americans during World War II. It provides funding to organizations that protect historic sites, record personal stories, and create educational tools that help the public understand what happened and why it matters today. The program serves communities, educators, museums, historians, descendants, and anyone seeking to learn about civil liberties, resilience, and the lived experiences of those affected.
items.uses: Japanese American Confinement Sites grant funds may be used for identifying, researching, evaluating, interpreting, protecting, restoring, repairing, and acquiring historic confinement sites where Japanese Americans were detained during World War II as authorized by the Preservation of Japanese American Confinement Sites Act of 2006. These historic confinement sites are defined as the ten War Relocation Authority camps (Gila River, Granada (Amache), Heart Mountain, Jerome, Manzanar, Minidoka, Poston, Rohwer, Topaz, and Tule Lake), as well as other historically significant locations, as determined by the Secretary of the Interior, where Japanese Americans were detained during World War II. It provides financial assistance for projects that help operate, maintain, and enhance National Scenic, National Historic, and National Recreation Trails. Funding supports activities that keep these nationally significant trail corridors safe, accessible, and culturally and environmentally respectful. The program helps partners carry out work such as trail operation and maintenance, resource protection, planning and trail development, interpretation and educational activities, and efforts that improve public understanding and enjoyment of the trails. Trail‑related digital platforms, data collection systems, and public outreach tools may also be supported to improve trail information, stewardship outcomes, and long‑term sustainability. Beneficiaries include the general public, nonprofit organizations, Tribal and community partners, landowners, and state and local governments. The program emphasizes volunteer engagement and supports partners working both inside and outside federally administered areas

items.title: Heritage Partnership
items.summary: The purpose of the Heritage Partnership Program funding is to carry out programs and projects that engage National Heritage Area (NHA) recipients, partners, communities, and/or visitors in shared environmental stewardship. It promotes greater public and private participation in preservation, conservation, education, and outdoor recreation programs and activities, and builds resource stewardship ethics in is…
items.description: The Heritage Partnership Program provides federal support to National Heritage Areas to preserve, interpret, and enhance nationally significant natural, cultural, historic, and recreational resources. It funds projects that strengthen environmental stewardship, promote public and private participation in preservation and education, and improve quality of life within designated heritage regions. Goals for each National Heritage Area are set forth in each of their designation legislation, but in general, the goal of designation as a National Heritage Area is to preserve and interpret for the educational and inspirational benefit of present and future generations the unique and significant contributions to our national heritage.
items.who: State, local, or tribal government or other public entity, an educational institution, or a private nonprofit organization.
items.uses: Funding and/or assistance is managed by an agency, nonprofit or other organized party identified in the public law that created the National Heritage Area. Funding is to accomplish intended purpose specified within each individual National Heritage Area's public law. Funding applies to interpretation and education, recreation, preservation and conservation and economic development of the region applied specifically to the nationally important story for which they were established.

This program provides grants for the acquisition and development within the Recreation Area of lands and waters or interests therein and provides cooperative agreements and/or technical assistance to enhance partner organization planning for and interpretation of non-Federal publicly owned lands within the Recreation…
items.description: This Assistance Listing is dedicated specifically to the 72‑mile Mississippi River corridor that flows through the Twin Cities region. It focuses on collaborative, community‑based conservation and encourages shared management through cooperative agreements and grants. Projects supported under this program help balance recreation, ecological health, cultural heritage, and urban community needs in one of the most significant urban national park units in the country.
items.who: The State of Minnesota or its political subdivisions.
items.uses: Funding and/or assistance is to be used by the State of Minnesota or its political subdivisions for the cost of acquisition and development within the Area of lands and waters or interest therein in a manner consistent with the legislation. Funding and/or assistance may be used to assist in the planning for and interpretation of non-Federal publicly owned lands within the Area and to develop and implement programs compatible with the comprehensive management plan.
contacts: Tavis Hill · Administrative Officer/Agreements Technical Representative · 314-296-9130 · tavis_hill@nps.gov

items.title: Natural Resource Stewardship
items.summary: The Natural Resource Stewardship program is the principle means through which the National Park Service (NPS) evaluates and improves the health of watersheds, landscapes, and marine and coastal resources, sustains biological communities on the lands and waters in parks, and actively endeavors to improve the resiliency of these natural resources. NPS conducts natural resource stewardship largely at the park level,…
items.description: This program provides federal financial assistance to eligible recipients to support conservation, research, restoration, and resource‑management activities that enhance natural resources managed by the National Park Service. Eligible applicants include tribal governments, state and local agencies, nonprofit organizations, institutions of higher education, and other qualified entities. Supported activities may include ecological research, habitat restoration, invasive‑species management, wildlife monitoring, public education, and stewardship actions aligned with federal priorities. The program emphasizes collaborative partnerships and science‑based approaches that deliver measurable public benefits.
items.who: State, local, or tribal governments, other Federal agencies, other public entities, educational institutions, private nonprofit organizations.
items.uses: Funds used for all aspects of natural resource (air, water, geological, biological) stewardship activities, including but not limited to resource inventories and monitoring, restoration projects, and wildlife and plant management. Funds may not be used for acquisition of real property.

items.title: Cooperative Research and Training Programs – Resources of the National Park System
items.summary: To establish and maintain cooperative study units, in partnership with federal, state, and local governments, tribes, nonprofit organizations, and institutions of higher education, to facilitate multi-disciplinary science and integrated information products related to the resources of the National Park System. To maintain a comprehensive network of cooperative study units that provide full geographic and topical…
items.description: The Cooperative Research and Training Programs support a nationwide network of university‑based study units that work with the National Park Service to address natural and cultural resource challenges. Through collaborative research, technical assistance, and education, the program helps develop practical, science‑based information that improves stewardship of parks and their surrounding landscapes. This assistance listing strengthens partnerships between academic institutions, researchers, students, and resource managers by funding projects that study wildlife, plants, water, air quality, historic sites, and other park resources. It also provides training opportunities for students and emerging professionals, expanding the scientific and technical workforce needed to care for public lands. The program serves state and local governments, tribal governments, nonprofit organizations, universities, conservation partners, researchers, communities, and the general public. What makes this program unique is its focus on cooperative, interdisciplinary science conducted through long‑standing partnerships that bring together local knowledge, academic expertise, and park management needs.…
items.uses: The objectives of the CESU program are: 1) Provide usable knowledge to support informed decision making; 2) Ensure the independence and objectivity of research; 3) Create and maintain effective partnerships among the Federal agencies and universities to share resources and expertise; 4) Take full advantage of university resources while benefiting faculty and students; 5) Encourage professional development of current and future Federal scientists, resource managers, and environmental leaders; and 6) Manage Federal resources effectively.
contacts: CESU Coordinator · National Coordinator · x · WASO_cesu@nps.gov

items.title: Cultural Resources Management
items.summary: The National Park Service (NPS) conducts cultural resource stewardship largely at the park level. Projects encompass a broad range of research, operational, and educational activities across all aspects of cultural resource stewardship, including but not limited to inventory, monitoring, research, rehabilitation, reconstruction, restoration, preservation, documentation, data recovery, and education.
items.description: The Cultural Resources Management listing supports projects that protect, document, and share the many stories, traditions, and materials that reflect our nation’s history and cultural heritage. Through cooperative agreements, the program helps communities and organizations care for historic objects, archives, archaeological sites, cultural landscapes, and traditional practices. Funding may support activities such as surveying and documenting cultural resources, preserving fragile materials, improving public access to collections, supporting educational programs, and strengthening community stewardship of cultural traditions. This listing serves a wide range of partners, including state and local governments, Tribal nations, nonprofit organizations, educational and scientific institutions, associations, and individuals working to preserve cultural resources for public benefit. These partners play a key role in expanding access to history, protecting culturally important places and objects, and making sure that the knowledge held in collections and cultural landscapes is passed on to future generations.
items.who: State, local, or tribal government or other public entity, an educational institution, or a private nonprofit organization.
items.uses: Funds used for all aspects of cultural resource stewardship activities, including but not limited to inventory, monitoring, research, rehabilitation, reconstruction, restoration, preservation, documentation, data recovery, and education. Funds may not be used for acquisition of real property.

items.title: National Fire Plan-Wildland Urban Interface Community Fire Assistance
items.summary: To assist communities at risk from catastrophic wildland fires by providing assistance in the following areas: community programs that develop local capability including; assessment and planning, mitigation activities, and community and homeowner education and action; plan and implement hazardous fuels reduction activities, monitoring or maintenance associated with such hazardous fuels reduction activities, on…
items.description: This program supports communities that are at risk from devastating wildland fires by helping them strengthen their local fire resilience and preparedness. The program provides funding for community-led efforts such as wildfire risk assessments, local mitigation planning, and education that helps residents understand how to protect their homes and neighborhoods. It also supports projects that reduce hazardous vegetation and fuels, either in nearby federal areas or on surrounding non-federal lands, to lessen the threat of severe fires in high‑risk regions. In addition, the program boosts opportunities for rural workers and small businesses and improves the capabilities of local fire districts through training and modern approaches to wildfire prevention. Through these combined efforts, the program advances the National Cohesive Wildland Fire Management Strategy while empowering communities, Tribal governments, states, local agencies, schools, and nonprofit organizations to build safer, more fire‑adapted places.
items.who: States and local governments at risk as published in the Federal Register or as determined by the state, Indian Tribes, public and private education institutions, nonprofit organizations.
items.uses: Hazard reduction activities are restricted to Federal lands, or adjacent nonfederal land for activities that benefit resources on Federal land. Assistance can be used to help the National Park Service support community based efforts addressing defensible space and fuels management issues; support outreach and education efforts associated with fuels management and risk reduction activities; and increase the effectiveness of rural fire protection.

items.title: National Park Service Conservation, Protection, Outreach, and Education
items.summary: This program supports projects complementary to National Park Service program efforts in natural and cultural resource conservation, protection, and environmental sustainability. This program funds projects that support the mission of the National Park Service but are not covered under other specific programs.
items.description: This program supports projects that help care for and protect the natural and cultural resources found on public lands while expanding opportunities for people to learn about and enjoy these places. Funding may be used for activities such as restoring habitats, preserving historic features, improving visitor access, and offering educational programs that connect communities with nature, history, and science. The program also helps strengthen environmental sustainability by supporting projects that reduce impacts to sensitive resources and promote responsible outdoor recreation. This assistance listing serves a broad group of partners, including nonprofit organizations, government entities, industry groups, researchers, and members of the public who benefit from healthier landscapes, improved access, and expanded learning opportunities.
items.uses: Applications must be for projects within the National Park Service area of responsibility. Funds may not be used for acquisition of real property.

items.title: Martin Luther King Junior National Historic Site and Preservation District
items.summary: The Martin Luther King, Junior, National Historic Site and Preservation District was established October 10, 1980 in order to protect and interpret for the benefit, inspiration and education of present and future generations the places where Martin Luther King, Junior, was born, where he lived, worked, and worshipped, and where he is buried.
items.description: This program supports the preservation and interpretation of the Martin Luther King, Jr. National Historic Site and Preservation District, a nationally significant area established to honor the life, work, and legacy of Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. Annual funding helps maintain operations, educational programs, and essential facilities at The King Center and surrounding park sites. These efforts ensure that the places where Dr. King was born, lived, worked, worshipped, and is laid to rest continue to educate and inspire people today and for generations to come.
items.uses: The Secretary may enter into cooperative agreements with the owners of properties of historical or cultural significance as determined by the Secretary, pursuant to which the Secretary may mark, interpret, improve, restore, and provide technical assistance with respect to the preservation and interpretation of such properties. Such agreements shall contain, but need not be limited to, provisions that the Secretary shall have the right of access at reasonable times to public portions of the property for interpretive and other purposes, and that no changes or alterations shall be made in the property except by mutual agreement. The authorities in this subsection shall also be available to the Secretary with respect to properties within the Martin Luther King, Junior, Preservation District.

items.title: Cooperative Management of Ebey's Landing National Historical Reserve.
items.summary: The objectives of this program focus on the cooperative management, administration, and protection of Ebey's Landing National Historical Reserve. They include overseeing land and facilities, administering conservation programs, and ensuring compliance with preservation measures. The work also involves coordinating with local governments, entering into partnerships and contracts, and securing funding to support the…
items.description: Ebey’s Landing National Historical Reserve is a unique place where history, rural landscapes, natural beauty, and community come together. Through this financial assistance program, the National Park Service works in partnership with the State of Washington and local governments to support the cooperative management of the Reserve, as directed by Public Law 95‑625. The program exists to help ensure that the Reserve’s historic farms, scenic views, cultural resources, recreational opportunities, and natural environments are protected and maintained for the benefit of the public. Unlike many national park units, Ebey’s Landing is managed through a shared governance model. The National Park Service can transfer certain management responsibilities to state or local partners, provide technical assistance, and offer supplemental funding to support day‑to‑day operations, long‑term preservation, and visitor services. These cooperative agreements strengthen local stewardship, allow communities to directly shape how the Reserve is cared for, and ensure that its rural heritage remains a living part of Island County.
items.who: The authorizing legislation for Ebey’s Landing National Historical Reserve states that the Secretary of Interior is authorized to transfer management and administration of the Reserve to an appropriate unit of local government. A joint administrative board called the Ebey’s Landing National Historical Reserve Trust Board (Trust Board), was created in accordance with the provision of RCW 39.34.030. The Trust Board consists of nine members: Three representatives of Island County, residing in the Reserve, three representatives from the Town of Coupeville, one [Washington] State Park representative, and one National Park Service representative. The Trust Board complies with the Open Public…
items.uses: The Ebey’s Landing National Historical Reserve was established in 1978 “to preserve and protect a rural community which provides an unbroken historical record from nineteenth century exploration and settlement in Puget Sound to the present time.” (National Parks and Recreation Act 1978, PL 95-625). The Trust Board of Ebey’s Landing National Historical Reserve was established to manage and administer the Reserve. The Trust Board is comprised of nine members, from Island County (3), Town of Coupeville (3), State Parks (1), and the National Park Service (1).

items.title: Emergency Supplemental Historic Preservation Fund
items.popular: HPF Disaster Relief Program; Emergency Supplemental Historic Preservation Fund Grants (ESHPF)
items.summary: The objectives of this supplemental funding is to provide for necessary expenses related to the consequences of disasters, including costs to States, Tribes, and territories. Funds may be used for historic and cultural resource preservation work in the program areas defined by the National Historic Preservation Act (54 USC 3001 et seq.) and that meets the Secretary of the Interior’s Standards and Guidelines for…
items.description: This Assistance Listing provides disaster recovery grants to support the preservation and repair of historic and cultural resources listed in or eligible for listing in the National Register of Historic Places or equivalent Tribal register. Funding may be used for preservation work eligible under the National Historic Preservation Act (54 USC 3001 et seq.) that also meets the Secretary of the Interior’s Standards and Guidelines for Archeology and Historic Preservation. Eligible projects include physical repairs to historic properties, survey and inventory of historic and cultural resources, compliance activities, disaster planning, and administrative and capacity support within areas receiving major disaster declarations. Funding should substantially mitigate disaster-caused damage and future risk.
items.who: Eligible applicants are defined as applicants in either the National Historic Preservation Act (54 USC 3001 et seq.), appropriations law and/or congressionally approved spending plans. They may include: State Historic Preservation Offices in the 50 states, 5 territories, 3 Freely Associated States, and District of Columbia (SHPOs); States; Tribal governments with signed Memorandum of Agreements with the National Park Service to assume the duties of the State Historic Preservation Office on Tribal lands, as defined in 54 USC 3001 et seq. (THPOs); Federally-recognized Tribes, Alaska Native Villages/Corporations, and Native Hawaiian Organizations as defined by 54 USC § 300309, 54 USC 300313…
items.uses: Emergency Supplemental Historic Preservation Fund (ESHPF) grants must be used to preserve historic and cultural resources located in areas that have received major disaster declarations and are listed in or eligible for listing in the National Register of Historic Places or similar Tribal register. Grants assist in physical repairs to historic properties, survey and inventory of historic and cultural resources, compliance activities, disaster planning, and administration activities necessary to carry out the preceding activities. All funded projects must follow the applicable Secretary of the Interior’s Standards and Guidelines for Archeology and Historic Preservation. In accordance with 54 USC 302902, grantees must agree to assume, after completion of a rehabilitation project, the cost of the continued maintenance, repair, and administration of the property in a manner satisfactory to…
